exam.name: NCMHCE
exam.whyThisModuleMatters: This module prepares learners to handle ethics and legal decision-making on the NCMHCE. Ethics items often test whether the counselor can prioritize client welfare, protect confidentiality, follow informed consent standards, recognize mandated reporting and duty-to-protect issues, maintain boundaries, document appropriately, and respond in the least harmful and most ethically defensible way.

intro.summary: This module covers the ethical and legal concepts most likely to appear on the NCMHCE, with emphasis on practical clinical decisions rather than abstract memorization. The focus is on what the counselor should do first, how to balance client welfare with legal duties, and how to choose the answer that is most protective, least harmful, and professionally defensible.
learningObjectives: Recognize the major ethical principles and how they guide clinical decisions
Understand the structure and practical use of the ACA Code of Ethics
Apply informed consent and confidentiality rules in clinical cases
Distinguish mandated reporting from duty to warn/protect
Identify best practices in documentation, supervision, and telehealth
Use an ethical decision-making model when a case is ambiguous
howToUse: Start with the ethics hierarchy and confidentiality section before moving into specific legal issues.
Study the difference between ethical obligations and state-law requirements, because the exam often tests both.
Read the case examples slowly. Ethics questions are often won by noticing one key fact such as a minor, a signed ROI, an identifiable victim, or a telehealth location issue.
When two answers both sound reasonable, choose the one that best protects client welfare while honoring law and professional standards.
highYieldThemes: Informed consent is ongoing, not one-and-done.
Confidentiality is central, but not absolute.
Mandated reporting and duty to protect are not the same thing.
Consultation, supervision, and documentation often strengthen the best ethical answer.
The exam usually rewards the least harmful and most clinically responsible action.

coreDecisionRules.example: If one answer preserves convenience but another better protects the client, the protective answer is usually stronger.

coreDecisionRules.rule: Clarify before disclosing whenever possible and clinically appropriate.
coreDecisionRules.example: If a client asks whether parents, a spouse, or insurance can access records, the best next step is often to review confidentiality limits through informed consent.
Imminent danger to self, imminent threat to an identifiable other, abuse reporting duties, and valid legal orders may require disclosure.

coreDecisionRules.rule: Do not confuse ethical best practice with legal minimums.
coreDecisionRules.example: A behavior may be legal in a jurisdiction but still ethically risky or unwise.
The exam often favors consultation with a supervisor, attorney, or ethics resource in complex dilemmas, followed by careful documentation.

ethicsHierarchy.title: Practical Ethics Hierarchy for the Exam
steps: Clarify informed consent and confidentiality limits
Identify legal obligations, including mandated reporting and protective duties
Apply the ACA Code of Ethics and relevant professional standards
Consult supervisors, colleagues, or legal resources when needed
Take the least harmful ethically and legally appropriate action
Document decision-making, rationale, consultations, and actions taken
examPearls: When the vignette is urgent, safety outranks routine process.
When there is no urgent danger, explanation, clarification, and consultation often come before drastic action.
Documentation is rarely the first step, but it is almost always part of the right plan.

acaCodeSection.title: ACA Code of Ethics Overview
acaCodeSection.overview: The ACA Code of Ethics is the main professional framework for counseling ethics. The NCMHCE does not test rote memorization of every subsection, but it does expect you to recognize which ethical theme is controlling the case: counseling relationship, confidentiality, competence, assessment, supervision, research, technology, or resolving ethical issues.

sections.practicalUse: Boundaries, client welfare, informed consent, roles, termination
Privacy, releases, exceptions, records, minor issues
Appropriate assessment use, cultural fairness, interpretation
Supervisory responsibility, client disclosure, trainee welfare
Research ethics, consent, participant protection, accurate reporting

sections.topic: Distance Counseling, Technology, and Social Media
sections.practicalUse: Telehealth, online boundaries, privacy, location and emergency planning
Consultation, addressing ethical violations, decision-making processes

examPearls: You do not need to quote section numbers to answer well, but you should know the themes.
Many exam answers can be improved by recognizing whether the issue is mainly confidentiality, boundaries, supervision, or technology-related.
howToUseOnExam: Identify the ethical category first: confidentiality, informed consent, boundaries, competence, assessment, supervision, technology, or legal duty.
Pair the code theme with applicable law and agency policy; do not treat the code as a substitute for mandated reporting or court requirements.
Choose the answer that protects client welfare, uses the least intrusive appropriate action, and includes consultation/documentation when the situation is complex.
Remember that ACA should be read as professional guidance for counselors, not as a guarantee that state laws are identical.
highYieldCodeThemes: A: Counseling relationship — client welfare, informed consent, boundaries, termination, referral, avoiding harm.
B: Confidentiality and privacy — privacy protection, releases, exceptions, records, group/family/minor complications.
C: Professional responsibility — competence, impairment, advertising, public statements, self-care, nondiscrimination.
D: Relationships with other professionals — collaboration, consultation, interdisciplinary care, appropriate information sharing.
E: Evaluation and assessment — proper tool selection, informed consent for assessment, cultural fairness, interpretation limits.
F: Supervision, training, teaching — supervisee competence, disclosure of trainee status, gatekeeping, role boundaries.
G: Research and publication — consent, participant protection, avoiding deception or misuse of data.
H: Distance counseling, technology, social media — telehealth consent, security, location, emergency planning, online boundaries.
I: Resolving ethical issues — ethical decision-making, consultation, addressing violations, documentation.

foundationalPrinciples.title: Foundational Ethical Principles

principles.name: Autonomy
principles.definition: Respecting the client's right to make their own decisions
principles.examUse: Important in informed consent, treatment choice, and respect for client agency

principles.name: Beneficence
principles.definition: Acting in the client's best interest
principles.examUse: Often supports proactive protective and helpful action

principles.name: Nonmaleficence
principles.examUse: Critical when weighing confidentiality, boundaries, risky interventions, and termination

principles.name: Justice
principles.examUse: Relevant to nondiscrimination, access, and consistent standards

principles.name: Fidelity
principles.definition: Trustworthiness, loyalty, and keeping professional commitments
principles.examUse: Important in alliance, boundaries, and reliable follow-through

principles.name: Veracity
principles.examUse: Relevant to informed consent, documentation, representation, and supervision

foundationalPrinciples.examPearl: When two answers seem close, the better one is usually the one that best preserves safety, trust, and fairness without creating avoidable harm.
foundationalPrinciples.overview: Foundational principles are the reasoning tools behind ethical answers. The exam often gives two tempting responses; principles help you decide which response protects the client while respecting rights, fairness, honesty, and professional trust.
howTheyShowUpOnExam: Autonomy supports informed consent, client choice, right to refuse treatment, and collaborative planning.
Beneficence supports active steps that help the client, especially when safety or functioning is at stake.
Nonmaleficence blocks actions that create avoidable harm, exploitation, abandonment, or boundary violations.
Justice requires fair access, nondiscrimination, cultural humility, and consistent standards.
Fidelity supports keeping professional commitments, maintaining trust, and following through on roles.
Veracity supports honest documentation, accurate credentials, truthful informed consent, and clear communication.
examApplication: If safety is urgent, beneficence and nonmaleficence usually outweigh routine confidentiality.
If no urgent risk exists, autonomy and fidelity often favor clarifying consent before acting.
If the counselor’s bias or values are central, justice and nonmaleficence point toward supervision, consultation, and avoiding value imposition.
If records, billing, credentials, or reports are involved, veracity becomes a major principle.

informedConsentSection.title: Informed Consent
informedConsentSection.overview: Informed consent is an ongoing process of explaining counseling, clarifying rights and responsibilities, and ensuring that the client understands the nature and limits of the service.
requiredElements: client right to ask questions and withdraw consent

specialSituations.bestPractice: Obtain parent/guardian consent when legally required and seek the minor's assent whenever possible
Involve legal decision-makers as needed while preserving the client's participation to the greatest extent possible
Clarify the counseling role, reporting expectations, and limits of confidentiality from the start
Include technology-specific consent, privacy risks, emergency procedures, and location requirements

examPearls: If a client asks who can access records, the best answer is often to clarify what can and cannot be shared.
Informed consent is not a single form; it is a continuing conversation.
When treatment conditions change, informed consent should be revisited.
examTraps: Assuming informed consent happened once at intake and never needs review
Overpromising absolute confidentiality
Ignoring the minor's understanding and participation entirely
clientRights: right to understand the nature and purpose of counseling
right to know risks, benefits, alternatives, fees, cancellation policies, and limits of confidentiality
right to ask questions and participate in treatment planning
right to refuse or withdraw from services when legally permitted
right to understand record access, privacy limits, and how information may be shared
ncmhceDecisionPoints: Review informed consent at intake, when treatment changes, when a new service is introduced, and when confidentiality questions arise.
For minors, distinguish parent/guardian legal rights from the minor’s clinical need for privacy and assent.
For court-ordered or mandated clients, clarify what information may be reported and to whom before treatment proceeds.
For telehealth, include technology risks, emergency procedures, backup contact methods, and client location.

confidentialitySection.title: Confidentiality and Privacy
confidentialitySection.overview: Confidentiality is one of the strongest foundations of counseling, but it is not absolute. Counselors must understand when information must be protected, when it may be shared with authorization, and when it must be disclosed because safety or law requires it.
coreRules: Protect client information unless there is valid authorization or a recognized exception
Disclose the minimum necessary information when disclosure is required
Clarify confidentiality limitations early and revisit them when needed
Use Release of Information (ROI) forms for voluntary disclosures

exceptionsMatrix.situation: Imminent risk of harm to self
exceptionsMatrix.typicalAction: Take protective action, which may include emergency services, hospitalization, support involvement, or other safety measures

exceptionsMatrix.situation: Imminent risk of harm to an identifiable third party
exceptionsMatrix.typicalAction: Duty to protect/warn may apply depending on jurisdiction; consult and act according to law and safety needs

exceptionsMatrix.situation: Suspected elder or dependent adult abuse

exceptionsMatrix.typicalAction: Respond according to legal requirement, ideally with consultation
Do not assume it equals an immediate full release; respond carefully and often consult legal/supervisory resources
Share only what is necessary and protect identifying details when possible
Explain that the counselor cannot fully guarantee other group members will keep disclosures private

examPearls: The exam often rewards clarifying and limiting disclosure rather than disclosing broadly.
Minimum necessary disclosure is a key concept.
A spouse, parent, employer, or school does not automatically get access without the proper legal/ethical basis.
confidentialityVsPrivilege: Confidentiality is the ethical/professional duty to protect client information.
Privilege is a legal protection against compelled disclosure in legal proceedings and may have exceptions or be waived.
A subpoena does not automatically mean the counselor releases everything; the counselor should follow law, agency policy, and legal consultation.
A court order carries more legal force than a routine request, but disclosure should still be limited to what is required.
recordsAccessRules: Payment by a spouse, parent, employer, or school does not automatically grant access to counseling records.
A signed ROI should specify what can be shared, with whom, for what purpose, and for what time period.
Share the minimum necessary information even when disclosure is allowed or required.
Group, couple, family, and minor counseling require extra clarity because more than one person may have privacy interests.

hipaaFerpaSection.title: HIPAA and FERPA Basics

hipaa.overview: HIPAA governs protected health information in many healthcare settings.
mustKnow: PHI includes identifying information connected to health or billing data
Provide Notice of Privacy Practices where applicable
Use secure systems and appropriate business associate agreements when needed
hipaa.examPearl: HIPAA is about privacy and protected health information, not a blanket excuse to refuse all communication.

ferpa.overview: FERPA protects educational records in school settings.
mustKnow: Educational records generally require consent for release
Parents usually have rights for minors, and students gain rights at adulthood as defined by the law
Health and safety emergencies can affect disclosure rules
ferpa.examPearl: FERPA applies to educational records, while HIPAA applies in healthcare contexts; the setting matters.

examDistinctions: HIPAA is usually healthcare privacy; FERPA is usually educational records in school settings.
The setting matters: a counselor in a school may face different record rules than a counselor in a clinic.
Neither HIPAA nor FERPA eliminates duties related to safety, mandated reporting, or valid legal process.
When unsure in a vignette, the safest answer often includes consultation and minimum necessary disclosure.

dutyToProtectSection.title: Duty to Warn / Duty to Protect
dutyToProtectSection.overview: When a client makes a serious threat against an identifiable person and appears capable of acting on it, the counselor may have a legal and ethical duty to take protective action.
coreElements: means or realistic ability to act
possibleProtectiveActions: warn the potential victim when legally required/permitted
consult supervisor, attorney, or agency policy resources
dutyToProtectSection.tarasoffConcept: The Tarasoff case established that therapist duties may extend beyond confidentiality when identifiable third parties face serious danger.
examPearls: The exam often expects recognition that a named target plus means plus credible threat changes the legal and ethical picture.
State law varies, but doing nothing is rarely the best answer when the threat is credible and serious.
examTraps: Treating all violent thoughts as equally serious without evaluating specificity
Ignoring access to means
Forgetting consultation and documentation
assessmentQuestions: Who is the target, and is the person identifiable?
Does the client have means, access, intent, plan, or recent escalation?
Is substance use, psychosis, domestic violence, or weapon access increasing danger?
What does state law, agency policy, supervision, or legal consultation require?

mandatedReportingSection.title: Mandated Reporting
mandatedReportingSection.overview: Mandated reporting is a legal duty, not merely a counseling option. Counselors must report suspected abuse or neglect in the categories recognized by law in their jurisdiction.
commonReportableConcerns: child emotional abuse where legally recognized
coreRules: Reasonable suspicion is generally enough; certainty is not required
The counselor does not investigate to prove the abuse before reporting
Failure to report can create professional and legal liability
examPearls: If a child is being harmed, the exam typically favors reporting rather than waiting for more proof.
The counselor may inform the client about the report when clinically safe and appropriate, but should not delay required reporting to negotiate with the client.
examTraps: Waiting for confirmation
Treating disclosure as a family problem rather than a reportable legal issue
Confusing adult domestic conflict with automatic mandated reporting when a child is not implicated
whatNotToDo: Do not investigate to prove the abuse before reporting.
Do not promise secrecy when reporting laws apply.
Do not delay a required report while trying to persuade the alleged abuser or family.
Do not treat reasonable suspicion as needing courtroom-level certainty.
afterReporting: Document the facts, report made, time, agency/contact, and consultation.
Continue clinical support when appropriate and safe.
Explain the report to the client or guardian when clinically appropriate without increasing danger.
Coordinate with supervisors or agency policy while keeping the client’s welfare central.

boundariesSection.title: Boundaries and Dual Relationships
boundariesSection.overview: Boundary issues are heavily tested because they often look subtle before they become clearly harmful. Counselors must avoid exploitative or impairing dual relationships and think carefully about role conflicts.

coreConcepts.definition: A secondary role with the client beyond counseling, such as friend, employer, teacher, business partner, or romantic partner
A departure from typical boundaries that may or may not be harmful depending on context
A harmful boundary breach that exploits or damages the client

clearlyProhibitedOrHighlyRisky: sexual or romantic relationship with a current client
dual roles that impair objectivity or harm the client
social media relationships that blur professional boundaries
using the client relationship for personal gain
imposing counselor personal values on client choices
inappropriate gift exchange that creates pressure or exploitation
self-disclosure that serves the counselor rather than the client
caseFactorsToEvaluate: whether the role can realistically be avoided
examPearls: The exam often favors avoiding the dual role when feasible.
When a boundary issue is unavoidable in a rural or community setting, the best answer usually includes consultation, transparency, documentation, and client protection.
examTraps: Assuming all boundary crossings are automatically ethical
Assuming all departures from standard practice are automatically unethical without context
Ignoring client vulnerability and power imbalance
commonVignettes: A client sends a friend request or direct message on social media.
A client offers an expensive gift or asks the counselor to attend a personal event.
A counselor in a rural area encounters unavoidable community overlap.
A counselor considers self-disclosure to meet their own emotional need rather than the client’s treatment goal.
A former client seeks a business, social, romantic, or financial relationship.
decisionChecklist: Does this primarily benefit the client or the counselor?
Could it impair objectivity, create dependency, or exploit the power difference?
Is the client vulnerable because of trauma, crisis, diagnosis, age, culture, or setting?
Can the boundary crossing be avoided or handled more safely?
Was the decision discussed, documented, and consulted on when needed?

supervisionSection.title: Supervision Ethics
supervisionSection.overview: Supervision-related ethics questions often test responsibility, competence, disclosure, and how supervisors should respond to impairment or risky practice.
corePrinciples: Supervisors bear responsibility for oversight of supervisee clinical work
Clients should know when they are seeing a supervised counselor or trainee
Supervisors must address supervisee impairment, incompetence, or unethical conduct
Sexual or exploitative relationships in supervision are unethical
examPearls: If a supervisee is unsafe or impaired, the supervisor must intervene rather than avoid conflict.
Client welfare outranks trainee comfort.
supervisionVsConsultation: Supervision includes evaluative responsibility and oversight of clinical work.
Consultation is usually advice-seeking among professionals and does not automatically transfer responsibility.
Supervisors must monitor competence, documentation, risk decisions, and ethical practice.
Supervisees should disclose limits, seek help early, and not practice beyond training.

documentationSection.title: Documentation Ethics and Legal Issues
documentationSection.overview: Good documentation protects clients, supports continuity of care, and provides a legal record of clinical reasoning and action.
mustKnowConcepts: clinical records typically belong to the practice or agency, but clients often have rights of access
psychotherapy/process notes may have greater protection than standard progress notes
records must be secure, accurate, and timely
retention periods vary by law and setting
documentation should cover intake, assessment, treatment planning, progress, crisis response, consultation, discharge, and referral
record storage and release practices must follow law, agency policy, and informed consent
bestPractices: record risk assessment and protective actions clearly
document consultation and rationale in ethical dilemmas
protect electronic records with secure systems
examPearls: If a case involves a difficult ethics decision, consultation and documentation often strengthen the best answer.
Documentation should be clinically useful and professionally defensible, not emotional or punitive.
examTraps: Charting broad unnecessary details when only minimum necessary disclosure is appropriate
Failing to document risk-related decisions and consultations
Confusing psychotherapy notes with general progress notes
whatToDocumentBySituation: Intake: presenting concern, consent, risk screen, relevant history, diagnosis impressions, plan.
Progress: client response, interventions, clinical reasoning, homework, next steps.
Risk: ideation, plan, intent, means, protective factors, safety plan, consultation, level-of-care decision.
Ethics/legal: facts, standards consulted, supervision/legal consultation, decision rationale, actions taken.
Discharge: reason for ending, progress, referrals, continuity plan, risk status.
badDocumentationPatterns: copy-paste notes that do not match the session
late or altered records without explanation

telehealthSection.title: Telehealth, Technology, and Social Media Ethics
telehealthSection.overview: Technology questions are increasingly important. The exam expects counselors to protect privacy, verify location, maintain emergency protocols, and preserve appropriate boundaries online.
mustDoInTelehealth: verify client location at time of session
have emergency and crisis procedures for remote care
practice within licensure and jurisdiction limits
socialMediaBoundaries: avoid casual friending/following that blurs the counseling relationship
do not discuss client material through insecure channels
aiAndTechnologyConsiderations: use technology ethically and transparently within professional standards
do not allow convenience to override confidentiality and competence
examPearls: Client location matters in telehealth because licensure is jurisdiction-based.
Emergency planning is part of competent telehealth practice, not an optional add-on.
examTraps: Starting telehealth without location verification
Using insecure platforms casually
Ignoring crisis planning because the client is remote
appropriatenessFactors: client risk level and ability to use remote care safely
emergency contacts and local crisis resources
clinical fit for the presenting problem and treatment modality
socialMediaExamRules: Maintain a professional social media policy and discuss it in informed consent when relevant.
Do not search for client information online casually unless there is a clinically justified safety reason and policy support.
Do not respond to crisis disclosures through public or insecure social media channels; move to appropriate emergency procedures.
Avoid online interactions that blur the counseling relationship or reveal client status.

assessmentAndEthicsSection.title: Assessment, Testing, and Ethics
assessmentAndEthicsSection.overview: When ethics questions involve assessment, the exam often tests whether the counselor chose an appropriate tool, used it competently, interpreted it carefully, and considered culture and fairness.
coreRules: use assessments that fit the referral question and client population
do not use tools beyond your competence
interpret results within cultural, linguistic, developmental, and contextual factors
avoid overpathologizing or overclaiming from limited data
examPearls: A technically valid tool can still be misused if it is not appropriate for that client or purpose.
Assessment ethics often intersect with informed consent and multicultural competence.
misuseExamples: using a test outside the counselor’s competence
making a diagnosis from one screening score alone
sharing raw results without appropriate explanation or consent

terminationSection.title: Termination, Referral, and Abandonment
terminationSection.overview: Termination questions often test whether the counselor is ending treatment responsibly or abandoning the client.
ethicalTerminationIncludes: planning and discussion of ending when possible
review of progress and ongoing needs
avoiding sudden unsupported withdrawal of services

abandonment.definition: Improperly ending counseling or failing to provide continuity or referral when the client still needs care
abandonment.examPearl: Abandonment is a major ethical problem. The counselor cannot simply disappear, stop responding, or terminate abruptly for personal convenience.

examTraps: Terminating in anger after conflict
Ending services because the client is difficult rather than because care is appropriately transferred
Refusing referral or coverage planning when the counselor becomes unavailable
appropriateReasonsToTerminateOrRefer: client needs a higher or different level of care
counselor lacks competence for the needed service
client is not benefiting despite appropriate efforts
agency/service limits require transfer with continuity planning
abandonmentWarningSigns: ending because the counselor is frustrated
no crisis coverage or transition plan
sudden termination after missed payment without ethical review
failure to respond to foreseeable risk during transition

ethicalDecisionMakingSection.title: Ethical Decision-Making Models
ethicalDecisionMakingSection.overview: When cases are ambiguous, the exam often rewards a process-based response rather than impulsive action.

models.name: Kitchener Hierarchy
steps: consult the ACA Code of Ethics
be aware of personal values and bias

models.name: ETHICS-A Model
steps: Select and implement the best action

ethicalDecisionMakingSection.examPearl: If the situation is complex and not urgent, consultation is often part of the best answer.
ncmhceStepByStep: Review ACA standards, law, agency policy, and informed consent.
Choose the least harmful ethically defensible action.
Document rationale, consultation, action, and follow-up.

commonExamTraps: Choosing a harsh or punitive response instead of a protective one
Confusing mandated reporting with duty to warn/protect
Disclosing too much information when only minimal necessary disclosure is justified
Ignoring consultation in a clearly complex ethics problem
Treating telehealth as ethically identical to in-person care
Forgetting to revisit informed consent when circumstances change
Mistaking a subpoena for an automatic full release without careful response

miniCaseDrills.case: A client asks whether their spouse can see therapy notes because the spouse pays for counseling.
miniCaseDrills.bestNextStep: Clarify confidentiality and record access rules through informed consent rather than agreeing automatically
miniCaseDrills.rationale: Payment does not automatically equal access.

miniCaseDrills.case: A parent reports that their partner has been hitting the child at home.
miniCaseDrills.bestNextStep: Make a mandated report according to law and agency procedure
miniCaseDrills.rationale: Reasonable suspicion of child abuse triggers reporting duty.

miniCaseDrills.case: A client says, 'I'm going to kill my ex-boss,' names the person, and describes having a weapon at home.
miniCaseDrills.bestNextStep: Treat as a serious protective-duty situation: assess immediacy, consult as needed, and take protective action consistent with law and safety needs
miniCaseDrills.rationale: Serious threat plus identifiable victim plus means changes confidentiality obligations.

miniCaseDrills.case: A telehealth client logs in from another state, and the counselor has no crisis contacts or emergency plan for that location.
miniCaseDrills.bestNextStep: Address jurisdiction and emergency planning issues immediately before continuing routine care
miniCaseDrills.rationale: Telehealth location and emergency readiness are essential ethical and legal considerations.

miniCaseDrills.case: A counselor in a small rural town is invited to the client's wedding, and declining may cause offense in a context where community overlap is common.
miniCaseDrills.bestNextStep: Evaluate risk of harm, consult, consider cultural/community context, maintain client welfare as primary, and document the decision
miniCaseDrills.rationale: Boundary decisions in unavoidable overlap settings require careful, contextual ethical reasoning.

memoryHooks: Confidentiality is strong but not absolute
Duty to protect = serious threat to identifiable other
finalTakeaways: The best ethics answer is usually the one that is safest, clearest, least harmful, and most professionally defensible.
Many ethics items are won by recognizing one turning-point detail: minor status, ROI, abuse suspicion, identifiable victim, or telehealth location.
Consultation and documentation do not replace action, but they often strengthen the right action.

checkpointQuestions.question: A client asks whether their parent, spouse, or insurer can automatically see therapy records. What is often the best next step on the exam?
checkpointQuestions.answer: Clarify confidentiality limits and access rules through informed consent

checkpointQuestions.question: What level of certainty is generally required before making a mandated abuse report?
What is the key difference between mandated reporting and duty to protect?
checkpointQuestions.answer: Mandated reporting concerns legally reportable abuse/neglect; duty to protect concerns serious danger to self or others, especially credible threats to identifiable third parties

checkpointQuestions.question: What should a counselor verify at the start of telehealth sessions that is especially important legally and ethically?
When a dilemma is complex but not immediately dangerous, what step often improves the most ethical answer?
checkpointQuestions.answer: Consultation with supervisor, colleague, attorney, or ethics resource

sourceBasis.notes: Expanded into a production-ready module emphasizing ethical principles, ACA Code themes, confidentiality, informed consent, protective duties, mandated reporting, boundaries, documentation, telehealth, and exam-style decision-making.

competenceScopeReferralSection.title: Competence, Scope of Practice, and Referral
competenceScopeReferralSection.overview: Competence questions test whether the counselor recognizes the limits of their training, credentials, supervision, and setting. The safest exam answer usually protects client welfare by seeking consultation, supervision, additional training, referral, or a higher level of care when the client need exceeds the counselor’s role.

mustKnowConcepts.definition: The services a counselor is trained, credentialed, supervised, and legally permitted to provide.
Actual ability to provide a service safely and effectively, not merely interest in the topic.
Connecting the client with a more appropriate provider or service when the counselor cannot meet the client’s needs.
A counselor condition such as burnout, substance use, illness, grief, or countertransference that interferes with safe practice.

whenToConsultOrRefer: The client presents with a specialty need outside the counselor’s training or supervision.
Risk level, psychosis, medical instability, or substance withdrawal requires a higher level of care.
The counselor’s values, bias, countertransference, or impairment may harm objectivity.
The setting cannot provide the service intensity, language access, accessibility, or cultural responsiveness the client needs.
A legal or ethical issue is complex enough that supervision, legal consultation, or agency policy review is needed.
examCues: New counselor + high-risk specialty presentation = consult/supervise before acting independently.
Personal discomfort alone is not an ethical reason to abandon or refer a client.
Referral should include continuity planning; the counselor does not simply end services abruptly.
Advocacy may be required when barriers, discrimination, or system issues interfere with client welfare.
examTraps: Assuming a license automatically makes the counselor competent for every population or technique.
Referring only because the counselor dislikes the client’s values or identity.
Continuing beyond competence without consultation because the counselor wants to help.
Ignoring counselor impairment, burnout, or countertransference when it affects care.
